title: Qlapoty: Improved analysis and eﬃciency for quaternionic ideal to isogeny transformation
authors: Max Duparc, Antonin Leroux, and Sina Schaeﬄer
abstract:
The quaternionic ideal-to-isogeny translation is a central building block of SQIsign. While the Qlapoti algorithm by Borin, Invernizzi, Corte-Real Santos, Eriksen, Mula, Schaeffler and Vercauteren significantly simplified and accelerated this step, it does not treat several technical details in sufficient depth, resulting in a flawed analysis of its failure probability. Additionally, several discrepancies between the implementation of Qlapoti and the paper's pseudocode were never analyzed explicitly. We address these shortcomings and add further improvements, resulting in a new norm equation solving algorithm with negligible failure probability. 
Our C implementations shows 6x to 9x speedups compared to Qlapoti's norm equation solver, and 1.3x-2.1x speedups for a SQIsign NIST2 signature (depending on NIST levels).

       Abstract. The quaternionic ideal-to-isogeny translation is a central build-
       ing block of SQIsign. While the Qlapoti algorithm by Borin, Invernizzi,
       Corte-Real Santos, Eriksen, Mula, Schaeffler and Vercauteren signifi-
       cantly simplified and accelerated this step, it does not treat several tech-
       nical details in sufficient depth, resulting in a flawed analysis of its failure
       probability. Additionally, several discrepancies between the implementa-
       tion of Qlapoti and the paper’s pseudocode were never analyzed explic-
       itly. We address these shortcomings and add further improvements, re-
       sulting in a new norm equation solving algorithm with negligible failure
       probability. Our C implementations shows 6x to 9x speedups compared
       to Qlapoti’s norm equation solver, and 1.3x-2.1x speedups for a SQIsign
       NIST2 signature (depending on NIST levels).

       Keywords: Isogenies, Quaternions, Ideal-to-Isogeny, SQIsign


1     Introduction
1.1   Context on ideal-to-isogeny translation
Isogeny-based cryptography is one of several approaches to modern post-quantum
cryptography. While it is not yet practically used, signature schemes like SQIsign [1]
and PRISM [5] offer the unique advantage of extremely small combined public
key and signature sizes, and SQIsign is currently in the 3rd round of the call
for additional post-quantum signatures by NIST [3]. This remains true even
in light of the recent improvements to the best known generic attacks against
isogeny-based cryptography introduced in [26].
    Both of these signatures are based on the Deuring correspondence [14], which
associates ideals in a quaternion algebra to isogenies between supersingular el-
liptic curves over a finite field. The secret quaternion ideals enable efficient com-
putation of the signature isogeny, while all public material consists in elliptic

to (public) isogenies and image curves is therefore a crucial building block of
signing and key generation.
    Ideal-to-isogeny subroutines have been the object of many improvements and
optimizations in the past years. The first instantiations of SQIsign [11,12] relied
on a generalization of the KLPT algorithm [18] to translate quaternion ideals
into smooth-norm quaternion ideals which could then be translated and com-
puted as one-dimensional smooth-degree isogenies. However, these isogenies had
very large degree and the computation was thus quite slow, with signing times in
the order of hundreds of milliseconds for the first NIST submission of SQIsign [8].
The development of the use of isogenies of 2- or 4-dimensional abelian varieties,
for embedding one-dimensional isogenies allowed to improve the performance
of the ideal-to-isogeny step, including in SQIsign, at the cost of more complex
mathematical objects. Inspired by ideas introduced in Clapoti [24] for quadratic
ideals, an efficient ideal-to-isogeny algorithm using two-dimensionnal isogenies
was introduced in [6], resulting in a SQIsign variant based on 2-dimensional iso-
genies [6] (other variants exist, such as [23,15] based on slightly different ideas).
These new quaternionic ideal-to-isogeny techniques later led to PRISM [5], which
cannot be instantiated using only smooth-degree one-dimensional isogenies, as
the required isogenies have large prime degree. The 2nd round NIST submission
of SQIsign [1] adapted [6] and the quaternionic version of Clapoti, but in or-
der to decrease the failure probability of the algorithm below 2−60 , important
complexifications were required. These modifications increased considerably the
memory requirement and the code complexity.
    In comparison, Qlapoti [7] simplifies the translation of quaternionic ideals
to isogenies considerably while reaching a better failure probability. In short, to
translate an ideal I of a special starting order O0 into an isogeny embedded in a
2-dimensional 2e -isogeny1 , it is necessary to find two ideals I1 , I2 both equivalent
to I and whose norms are such that


                                   n(I1 ) + n(I2 ) = 2e .                               (1)

   This step is referred to as the norm equation step. Then the endomorphism
θ described by the product I2 I¯1 is evaluated at the special starting curve E0
and the image determines the kernel of the 2-dimensional 2e -isogeny through
which the isogeny associated to I can be evaluated. We refer to this part as
the isogeny-side of the ideal-to-isogeny translation. The main improvement of
Qlapoti over the previous approach using Clapoti adaptations is that it gives
an algorithm to solve exactly Eq. (1), while the Clapoti adaptations required to
add additional scalar factors which made the isogeny side of the ideal-to-isogeny
translation more complex and costly. Additionally, the norm equation solving
algorithm in Qlapoti is fairly simple, compared to previous approaches.

1.2   Shortcomings of Qlapoti and our improvements
Despite its attractiveness, the Qlapoti algorithm as presented in [7], exhibits se-
rious drawbacks. We give a list of shortcomings that motivated our work, which
addresses these issues.

     1. The norm equation algorithm as described in the paper does not enforce
that the solution translates to a computable 2e -isogeny, since, if n(I1 ) and n(I2 )
are even, no kernel basis can be computed. Additionally, it does not guarantee
that the first (2, 2)-isogeny step of the two-dimensional isogeny to be computed
is a gluing isogeny, i.e. an isogeny from a product of elliptic curves to an abelian
variety which is not such a product. Handling non-immediate gluing requires
to work with xy-arithmetic, thus leading to more complex isogeny code and

variable-length 2e length 2-dimensional isogenies after the non-gluing steps,
which are more difficult to optimize. Finally, as the norm equation side costs
little compared to the isogeny side, it makes sense to handle additional com-
plications on this faster side by rejecting unsuitable norm equation solutions.
While the implementation section of Qlapoti mentions these issues, and their
C implementation of the norm equation solver adresses it (which is necessary
for its integration in the SQIsign NIST implementation’s optimized code), the
impact of these modification was not studied in the paper.
    → We fill in this gap by providing a norm equation solver ensuring computable
isogenies and immediate gluing at a minimal cost.
    2. The pseudocode presented in [7] is not optimized and not faithful to what
is implemented. As a consequence, the impact of several of the optimizations
used in the implementation are not properly analyzed. Furthermore, even with
these optimizations, the norm equation step remains quite inefficient for some
parameter sets. In particular for the SQIsign parameter set called Level 3, the
norm equation solver from [7] takes nearly half of the runtime of the signing
procedure.
    → We provide an optimized implementation of our algorithm which outper-
forms the previous implementation by a factor 5 to 9. Contrarily to Qlapoti, the
pseudocode we provide and analyze matches closely what we implemented, up to
tiny and clearly stated changes which can only improve its success probability.
    3. The analysis of the failure probability of Qlapoti makes some assumptions
which are too optimistic. In particular, the failure probability estimate given in
[7, Table 3], is based on the heuristic that the minima of a two-dimensional lattice
appearing in some part of the algorithm is following the Gaussian heuristic, which
we show is false. This oversight cascade into some failure probability estimates
that do not reflect the reality of the algorithm.
    → We provide a thorough analysis of our new algorithm, including all its
optimizations, and prove under plausible and experimentally verified heuristics
that the failure probability is negligible for parameters relevant for cryptography,
as shown in Table 1. Following this analysis, we believe the numbers presented
in [7, Table 3] are off by a factor of at least 264 .

1.3     Outline of the paper

In order to achieve the improvements listed above, we modified almost every
step in the norm equation solver of Qlapoti, resulting in a new algorithm we call
Qlapoty. 2
    In Section 2, we define most notations and provide the necessary background
on quaternions to understand the norm equation algorithm, of which we provide
a detailed overview in Section 2.2. At a high level, we explain how the norm
equation solver can be divided into two consecutive steps or loops (as they both
iterate over a set of candidates until some suitable element is found). The input
of the second loop is essentially the output of the first loop. We will treat and
analyze these two loops somewhat independently.
    We start with our variant of the second step of the algorithm in Section 3.
In particular, this is where we enforce the geometric conditions efficiently. We
identify a precise set of conditions on its input for this loop to succeed with high
probability. Then, we explain in Section 4 when and how the input conditions
of the second step can be met.
    Finally, we put our two building blocks together to obtain our algorithm
Qlapoty and analyze its global failure probability in Section 5. Benchmarks of
our C implementation are given in Section 6.


Related work. While this work was finalized, we became aware of an indepen-
dent and concurrent work [19] on improving Qlapoti. Interestingly, the proposed
solutions are quite unrelated to ours. Indeed, most of that work focuses on ex-
ploiting all optimization possibilities provided by the extended Cornacchia algo-
rithm. In contrast, our works minimise the use of the Cornacchia algorithm, so
that we could use a Cornacchia algorithm working only on prime inputs without
issues. For that reason, our improvements are more or less incompatible with the
ones proposed in [19]. Furthermore, [19] does not address the non-immediate glu-
ing problem and therefore works with variable length 2-dimensional isogenies,
which is undesirable as explained above. Finally, it does not improve on the
failure analysis of [7] and therefore suffers from the same issues.

2.2   Qlapoti
For a full exposition of Qlapoti and its norm equation, we refer to the pa-
per [7]. Below we fix some notations for the rest of this article while providing
an overview of the algorithm. A precise description of the algorithm, following
closely [7], is given in Algorithm 5.

Goal of the algorithm. Qlapoti has two main parameters: the prime charac-
teristic p, and an exponent e. On input a left O0 -ideal J in Bp,∞ , the goal is to
find I1 ∼ J and I2 ∼ J such that n(I1 )+n(I2 ) = 2e . This is equivalent to solving
the norm equation n(β1 ) + n(β2 ) = 2e n(I) with β1 , β2 ∈ I for some I ∼ J. The
Qlapoti algorithm can find solutions to this equation efficiently when p/2e is not
too big (at most logarithmic in p).
    This allows to embed the isogenies corresponding to the ideals I1 , I2 into a 2-
dimensional 2e -isogeny that can be efficiently computed from the endomorphism
θ := β2 · β1 /n(I) ∈ O0 . To help with that computation, 2e+2 torsion points are
useful, so we consider henceforth that p = 2e+2 f − 1 for some small odd f .

Overview of the algorithm. The first step of the algorithm is to compute
I, the smallest equivalent ideal to its input J. This ideal I is where all the
computations will be made. The norm of I will always be denoted N .

While always theoretically possible from a pair of suitable ideals I1 , I2 , the prac-

    As a result, some solutions are rejected during the norm equation solving
